newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress lambasts government on economy.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress lambasts government on economy.

text.p: India's Congress party, which provides crucial support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority coalition, slammed his economic policies on Friday but did not say if it would block the government's annual budget.

"Serious concern was expressed at the hike in prices, about the drift in the economic situation and its management," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told reporters after a meeting of the Congress Parliamentary Party's executive committee.
"Foreign investments are going down, industrial production is slowing down and there is a sharp fall in the rate of exports," Gadgil said.
Deve Gowda's United Front alliance was holding a separate meeting to discuss its strategy for the budget session of parliament which is expected to start on February 20.
Later on Friday, senior United Front leaders took stock of the political situation arising out of growing differences with the Congress party, the United News of India (UNI) said.
The news agency said Deve Gowda explained to his colleagues that his office had no role to play in the interrogation of Congress president Sitaram Kesri by the federal police last Sunday.
The Congress had lambasted the government earlier this week after federal investigators questioned Kesri to probe a complaint by a former aide that some of his assets were not properly accounted.
Analysts said the uneasy alliance between Deve Gowda and Kesri could hit a flashpoint in debate over the budget for fiscal 1997/98 ending March 31.

Deve Gowda, with fewer than 200 supporters in the 545-seat Lok Sabha (lower house of parliament), needs the support of the 137 Congress deputies to beat off a relentless challenge from the main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
But Congress, which was ejected from power by the United Front following general elections in May last year, was careful not to take an openly confrontational stand.
"Do not jump to conclusions," Gadgil said when asked if the Congress criticism of Deve Gowda's economic policies signalled a falling-out over the budget.
"This is not a meeting to decide if the Congress will or will not withdraw its support to Deve Gowda," one Congress official told Reuters.
"We have to brief our members of parliament about what we think of our support to the government so far."

Industrial growth slowed to 9.8 percent in April-September 1996 compared with 12.1 percent a year earlier. Inflation, measured by the wholesale price index, hit 7.75 percent on January 4, a 58-week high.
The Planning Ministry estimates gross domestic product growth in 1996/97 will slow to 6.5 percent after 7.1 percent the previous year.
